transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-06
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Redwood SRE), Jordan Blake (Elysium VP of ML), Camille Ruiz (Elysium SRE), Omar Lee (Elysium Platform), Tessa N'Goma (Elysium ML Eng)

Summary:
Technical deep dive on GPU runtime profiling: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graphs, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, and quantization impact. Discussed on-prem/VPC constraints and next steps for pilot and benchmarks.

Topics:
- Kernel selection heuristics and fallback
- TensorRT-LLM profiling vs vLLM (throughput/latency, p50/p95/p99)
- CUDA Graphs effects on launch overhead and dynamic sequences
- KV cache impacts on memory and multi-request latency
- Batching strategies (dynamic batching, batching windows, fairness)
- Quantization profiles and perf/quality tradeoffs
- VPC/on-prem deployment constraints (KMS, networking, GPU isolation)

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex: All right folks, thanks for joining. We'll keep this fairly technical — Priya and Liam will walk through the profiling we ran, and then Jordan and team can show the sample workload you sent.
[00:00:30] Jordan: Sounds good. Quick note — our main goal is to understand where the p95/p99 latency comes from with our 8k-seq prompts and whether TensorRT-LLM gives consistent advantage over the v-l-l-m stack.
[00:00:45] Priya: yep that's our goal too. We ran matched experiments on A100 and H100-ish hardware, with and without cudagraphs, and with different kernel selection flags. We'll share the spreadsheet.
[00:01:15] Camille: when you say "kernel selection flags" do you mean autotuned kernels inside TRT or something on the runtime side?
[00:01:30] Priya: Both, a little. TensorRT-LLM will pick TRT kernels, but our runtime also selects between fused-attention kernels and fallback slower kernels depending on sequence length and quantization. Sometimes the runtime picks a more conservative kernel which hurts p50 but stabilizes p99.
[00:01:55] Liam: and that selection is driven by heuristics we maintain — sequence length distribution, kv cache hit rates, and observed memory pressure.
[00:02:10] Omar: we've seen strange regressions when kv cache gets large — it bloats GPU memory and then the allocator triggers a different path — is that what you mean by memory pressure?
[00:02:25] Priya: Exactly. We noticed that when KV cache grows beyond the fast allocation pool, allocation latency spikes and then kernels are forced into an alternate code path. We sometimes call that the KV cash path in notes (laughs) — transcription sometimes writes KV cash.
[00:02:45] Jordan: ha, yes we've seen that. So what were the numbers — does TRT-LLM reduce p99 vs vLLM?
[00:03:00] Priya: Short answer: on throughput for large batches, TRT-LLM wins by 20-35% on tokens/sec for FP16/INT8 quantized models, but for dynamic single-request low-latency scenarios vLLM with optimized fused-kernels can be competitive. The big wins come when using CUDA Graphs to remove kernel launch overhead and when the KV cache fits the preferred allocation region.
[00:03:35] Alex: we have a slide with a microbench; Priya, can you show the raw traces?
[00:03:45] Priya: sure. (screen) here's a timeline from our profiler — you can see launch stalls at the start of each iteration when not using cudagraphs. When we record the graph and replay, the launch overhead disappears but you need static-ish shapes or staged recording to amortize.
[00:04:10] Tessa: that's one concern — our workload has variable sequence lengths, multiple users with different prompts. How brittle is cudagraphs with dynamic seq lengths?
[00:04:25] Priya: it's brittle if you try a naive single recording. Best practice is to record multiple graphs for representative shapes and switch between them, or use partial graphs for the stable portions like attention and cache update. There's also overhead for switching graphs but it's small compared to per-kernel launch on hot paths.
[00:04:50] Jordan: ok, and what about quantization — you mentioned INT8. How much quality loss did you see?
[00:05:05] Priya: it's model dependent. For some Llama-variant we saw <1% BLEU-style drop on our eval set at post-training static INT8 with per-channel calibration. For others, mixed precision (FP16) preserved quality and still gave a decent perf bump. We recommend evals on your prompt-suite before committing.
[00:05:30] Camille: and is the kernel selection different for INT8 vs FP16?
[00:05:40] Liam: yes, some fused kernels are not available in INT8, and TRT will pick optimized INT8 kernels where available. Our runtime's kernel selector marks kernels with a capability tag and then prefers specialized kernels when available and safe.
[00:06:00] Alex: let's zoom into a specific case — 4k context, KV cache warm, batching at small windows (N=4). Priya, what happened there?
[00:06:15] Priya: With small batching windows, vLLM's continuous batching gives lower tail latencies because it streams KV cache more efficiently. TRT-LLM with cudagraphs did well on throughput but had a higher p99 due to graph switch overhead and occasional memory compactions.
[00:06:40] Jordan: memory compactions? what triggers that?
[00:06:45] Priya: the allocator tries to reduce fragmentation when free regions drop below threshold; that can trigger memcpy-like operations which bump latency. On H100 with unified memory tuning it's less frequent, but on older A100 nodes it's more noticeable.
[00:07:05] Omar: do you have mitigation suggestions?
[00:07:10] Priya: yes — maintain a reserve allocation pool for KV cache footprint, tune the caching policy to evict cold keys earlier, and for TRT workflows pre-reserve workspace for worst-case so you avoid allocator stalls. Also we recommend setting a conservative graph-switch debounce so you don't switch graphs on every small shape variance.
[00:07:35] Tessa: on the topic of KV cache size, do you have numbers on how memory scales? For 8k tokens, per-request KV is roughly X bytes?
[00:07:50] Priya: ballpark: for a 7B-ish model, KV cache is ~2-3 bytes per token per head per layer aggregated; practically we saw ~1.8GB for an 8k context on 8-bit quantized flavor. It varies with heads/layers. We'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[00:08:15] Jordan: great. Now on latency SLOs, we're targeting 200ms p95 for short completions — is that realistic on our infra?
[00:08:30] Liam: depends on batching and concurrency. For single-shard with H100 and optimized FP16 kernels + cudagraphs, 200ms p95 is achievable for short generations (<128 tokens) if you limit multi-tenancy and reserve a small burst pool. But multi-tenant noisy neighbors will push p95 above that.
[00:08:55] Camille: that ties into VPC/on-prem concerns — we need predictable isolation and no noisy neighbor. Does Redwood have a recommended dedicated capacity config?
[00:09:05] Alex: yes, Redwood Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and autoscaling policy with burst limits. For on-prem we can recommend node pinning, cgroup isolation, and GPU partitioning if supported. We'll share an infra checklist.
[00:09:25] Jordan: good. Back to kernel selection — are there scenarios where vLLM picks a faster kernel than TRT-LLM?
[00:09:40] Priya: yes, especially with small sequence-length distributions and streaming generation. vLLM's continuous aggregation and fused attention kernels are highly optimized for streaming; TRT-LLM shines when you can batch many sequences with similar shapes and leverage tensor core kernels. If your workload is chatty and single-request heavy, vLLM can be better.
[00:10:05] Omar: any notes about model compilation time? TRT-LLM requires a building/compilation step, right?
[00:10:15] Priya: correct. TensorRT-LLM has an ahead-of-time compilation/optimization pass that can take minutes per model/shape configuration. That's another operational cost: maintain compiled artifacts per model variant + quantization profile. vLLM tends to be faster to iterate with.
[00:10:35] Tessa: hmm that affects our CI/CD for model rollouts. Do you support automated artifact management?
[00:10:45] Alex: Redwood's platform can manage compiled artifacts and tie them to model versions and rollouts — we keep graph artifacts in the control plane and can push them to Dedicated/Private nodes. We'll include the artifact lifecycle doc.
[00:10:58] Jordan: good. Can we talk about perf delta numbers — do you have a quick table?
[00:11:05] Priya: yes — quick numbers from our test: on H100, 7B model, FP16: vLLM throughput 12k tokens/s, TRT-LLM 15k tokens/s (+25%). With INT8 quantization TRT-LLM went to 18k tokens/s (+50% vs vLLM. but quality delta 0.8% on our eval). p99s: vLLM 320ms, TRT-LLM 410ms without graph switching optimizations, with cudagraphs TRT p99 drops to ~280ms in batched workload.
[00:11:45] Camille: interesting — so cudagraphs is a big enabler for p99 improvement on TRT.
[00:11:50] Priya: correct. But again, cudagraphs requires careful management for variable-length requests.
[00:12:05] Jordan: how much engineering effort to maintain multiple graphs per shape?
[00:12:15] Liam: initial setup maybe a couple weeks to integrate recording, graph store, and selector rules. Maintenance is mostly around adding shapes for new prompt patterns. Our Optimize tooling can suggest which shapes to capture based on token distribution.
[00:12:35] Tessa: you mentioned Optimize — can it recommend quantization settings and batching windows?
[00:12:45] Alex: yes, Redwood Optimize looks at your token distribution and latency/cost targets and recommends batching window sizes, quantization profiles, and whether to prefer TRT or vLLM for a given route. We'll demo that in the pilot.
[00:12:58] Jordan: perfect. Security question — if we do on-prem with KMS, how do key operations work?
[00:13:05] Alex: we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). For private deployments, the keys remain in your KMS and we do not persist plaintext model artifacts in our control plane. We'll send the security checklist and SOC2 docs.
[00:13:20] Camille: please include audit log examples for inference requests.
[00:13:25] Alex: will do.
[00:13:30] Priya: back to profiling — one more thing: kernel fallback behavior. When a custom fused kernel fails (e.g., unsupported shape), the runtime falls back to a reference kernel which is functionally correct but slower. These fallbacks often explain spikes in p99. We instrumented fallbacks in the tracing and you can filter traces to find them.
[00:13:55] Jordan: nice. Do you provide automatic fallback alerts?
[00:14:00] Priya: yes, Redwood Console will surface kernel fallbacks, graph re-records, and allocation churn as alerts. You can tie those to regressions on your eval prompt suites.
[00:14:15] Tessa: about eval prompt suites — we'll share ours. What's the best format?
[00:14:20] Alex: a CSV with prompt, expected token length, and a small set of gold outputs works. For quality diffs we run side-by-side comparisons and generate delta metrics.
[00:14:35] Omar: any gotchas on multi-GPU? We plan to shard KV across multiple GPUs.
[00:14:45] Priya: sharding KV is standard for long contexts. Be mindful of cross-GPU bandwidth on NVLink; interconnect latency can show up in tail p99. For multi-GPU, cudagraphs that span multiple GPUs are trickier but possible; you need careful synchronization.
[00:15:05] Jordan: and for model parallel > single device, does TRT-LLM support that well?
[00:15:15] Priya: TRT has good multi-GPU support but orchestration is more involved. vLLM can be simpler for horizontal sharding in some cases. We'll map out tradeoffs for your topology.
[00:15:30] Alex: ok I'm going to open the profiler trace for a case Jordan provided — 8k context, mixed prompt sizes, concurrency 6.
[00:15:40] (screen share)
[00:15:50] Priya: see here — frequent graph switches at ~00:16:20 correlate with increased p99. At ~00:17:05 there's an allocation stall tied to GC-like compaction. Those are the two root causes.
[00:16:10] Jordan: is there any quick win to reduce those?
[00:16:15] Priya: reserve workspace, record graphs for the most common shapes, and set a per-route batching policy to reduce shape diversity under the same worker.
[00:16:30] Camille: about batching policies — can Redwood enforce per-route batching windows?
[00:16:35] Alex: yes, per-route config with max latency window and max batch size; you can also set fairness constraints.
[00:16:45] Tessa: what's the overhead of per-route policies on throughput?
[00:16:50] Liam: negligible — the routing decision is cheap. Contention arises if you misconfigure windows (too small to fill) or set incompatible max batch sizes.
[00:17:05] Jordan: digging into CUDA Graphs — do you have tips for debugging when graph replay yields wrong outputs?
[00:17:15] Priya: common causes are non-deterministic ops, or when you forget to include ephemeral buffers in the capture. Best practice: validate graph outputs against the interpreter for representative inputs and run a few iterations comparing logits.
[00:17:30] Omar: any improvements in graph switching overhead in newer CUDA versions?
[00:17:35] Priya: CUDA 12+ made some improvements but graph switch still costs non-zero, particularly when you reconstruct many small graphs. The trend is better, but you should still design for amortizing cost.
[00:17:50] Jordan: can Redwood's runtime automate graph selection?
[00:17:55] Priya: partially. We can pick the best graph based on request shape histograms and a cost model. Fully automated graph recording needs integration with your CI to add new shapes.
[00:18:10] Alex: quick poll — is the customer leaning toward TRT-LLM for throughput or vLLM for latency-sensitive interactive? Jordan?
[00:18:20] Jordan: leaning hybrid — TRT for batch-heavy embedding/generation pipelines, vLLM for chatty low-latency routes. But we want to quantify that with your pilot.
[00:18:35] Camille: agreed. For regulatory reasons we might also prefer on-prem for certain datasets.
[00:18:40] Alex: that's fine — we support Private deployments and can run the same runtime there. We'll send the private deployment checklist.
[00:18:50] Tessa: one more thing — can you include examples of when kernel fallback triggered and the stack trace in the trace export?
[00:18:58] Priya: yes we'll include annotated traces with fallback reasons.
[00:19:05] Jordan: great, this is helpful. Any other perf tunables we should consider?
[00:19:10] Priya: adjust tensor core tile sizes, set per-model workspace, tune batching debounce, and quantization calibration technique. Also look into prewarming for cold starts.
[00:19:25] Omar: do you prewarm graphs automatically on node boot?
[00:19:30] Liam: we provide prewarm hooks; you can configure a set of representative inputs to warm caches and graphs. This avoids first-request latency spikes.
[00:19:45] Camille: ok that's important.
[00:19:50] Alex: shifting gears — deployment ops: how large are compiled artifacts and how are they stored?
[00:19:55] Priya: compiled TRT artifacts can be tens to hundreds of MB depending on shape variety. We store them in the artifact store and push to nodes with checksums. For air-gapped infra we support on-prem artifact distribution via secure bundle.
[00:20:12] Jordan: would love an estimate for our model sizes.
[00:20:15] Priya: we'll include that in benchmark spreadsheet.
[00:20:20] Tessa: about observability — can we get token-level traces and p99 breakdowns?
[00:20:25] Alex: yes Redwood Console has token-level cost and latency breakdowns and per-route dashboards. We can also stream traces to your preferred tracing backend.
[00:20:40] Jordan: excellent.
[00:20:45] (long profiling silence as screen is shared - 00:20:45 to 00:34:00 — deep dive reviewing traces)
[00:34:05] Priya: back — we've annotated the traces. Key takeaways: (1) cudagraphs reduce launch stalls substantially; (2) kernel fallbacks and allocation compactions explain most p99 spikes; (3) TRT-LLM gives throughput advantage for batched workloads especially with INT8; (4) vLLM is better for streaming single-tenant interactive flows.
[00:34:35] Jordan: sounds right. What are expected engineering times for the pilot?
[00:34:40] Alex: for a remote pilot on your VPC we estimate 2-4 weeks: week 1 instrument + baseline; week 2 run TRT-LLM/vLLM side-by-side; week 3 tune graphs/quant; week 4 finalize recommendations. On-prem may add extra time for air-gap and KMS.
[00:35:05] Camille: can you do the pilot with limited access to our VPC? We prefer SCIM/SAML and limited roles.
[00:35:15] Alex: yes we support least privilege service accounts and we can pass a minimal RBAC checklist.
[00:35:25] Omar: can you also provide cost estimates for Dedicated vs self-hosting?
[00:35:30] Alex: we'll include a cost model — tokens/sec * instance-hour and amortized compiled artifact ops.
[00:35:45] Jordan: last question — any gotchas with model updates? If we retrain and change head sizes, do we recompile graphs?
[00:35:55] Priya: if architecture changes or heads/layers differ you'll need new compiled artifacts and likely new graphs. Small weight updates don't require recompilation unless they change shapes. We'll recommend a CI step to detect shape changes and trigger artifact rebuilds.
[00:36:20] Tessa: bet. That addresses our concerns.
[00:36:25] Alex: ok to recap next steps?
[00:36:30] Jordan: go ahead.
[00:36:35] Alex: Next steps: 1) Alex will send benchmark spreadsheet and annotated traces by 2026-05-10; 2) Elysium to share sample prompts and token distribution by 2026-05-12; 3) Redwood to propose pilot dates for the week of 2026-05-18; 4) Priya to prepare pilot infra checklist by 2026-05-14.
[00:37:00] Jordan: confirmed.
[00:37:05] Camille: please also send SOC2 and audit log examples.
[00:37:10] Alex: will do.
[00:37:15] (closing notes and small chit-chat)
[00:38:00] Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.
[00:38:10] Jordan: thanks, bye.
[00:38:15] (call ends)
